events.description: On August 13, 1521, Cuauhtémoc attempted to escape the fallen city by canoe with a small group of nobles and family. He was intercepted by a Spanish brigantine, captured, and brought before Cortés — and the city surrendered the same day, ending the Aztec Empire.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: According to Aztec oral tradition, when Cuauhtémoc was brought before Cortés he reportedly said: "I have done everything in my power to save my kingdom and my people, and I have failed. Do with me as you will." Cortés had him tortured with boiling oil to locate Aztec gold reserves, kept him alive for four years as a political hostage, and finally executed him in 1525 — Cortés later called it a mistake. Modern Mexico venerates Cuauhtémoc as a symbol of indigenous resistance; there is no equivalent monument to Cortés.

events.label: Templo Mayor Phase II
events.description: The Templo Mayor underwent its second major construction phase during the reigns of Acamapichtli and Huitzilihuitl, when the original modest shrine was significantly enlarged with new stone facings and stairways — establishing the twin-staircase profile that would define all subsequent expansions.

events.label: Templo Mayor Phase IV
events.description: The fourth construction phase of the Templo Mayor, undertaken during Motecuzoma I's reign, was the most architecturally ambitious to that point — raising the twin pyramid to over 30 meters, adding the Coyolxauhqui stone at the base of the Huitzilopochtli stairway, and constructing the surrounding sacred precinct with new auxiliary temples.

events.label: Tenochtitlan Sacred Precinct
events.description: The Sacred Precinct (Huey Teocalli) at the center of Tenochtitlan was a walled ceremonial compound of over 78 structures by 1500, anchored by the Templo Mayor and including temples, a skull rack (tzompantli), a ball court, and elite schools — the religious and political heart of the empire.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Tenochtitlan was founded on an island in Lake Texcoco in the Basin of Mexico around 1325, growing from a marshy island settlement to a city of perhaps 200,000–300,000 people by the early 16th century — one of the largest cities in the world at the time. The entire city was organized around the Sacred Precinct; four causeways radiated outward from the precinct walls to connect the island to the mainland, and the grid of streets and canals was oriented to the precinct's alignment. When the Spanish demolished the precinct after 1521, they built the Mexico City Cathedral directly over the Templo Mayor's foundations.

events.label: Quetzalcoatl Return Prophecy
events.description: Quetzalcoatl ("Feathered Serpent") was one of the most important deities in the Aztec pantheon — god of wind, Venus, merchants, knowledge, and the priesthood — whose mythological departure eastward across the sea and promised return in a year called One Reed (corresponding to 1519) haunted Motecuzoma II as the Spanish arrived.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Among the Aztecs, Quetzalcoatl was also closely associated with the planet Venus as both morning and evening star, and with the wind god Ehecatl. The legend of his departure and return predates the Aztecs, appearing in Toltec tradition, and was likely not understood as a literal political prophecy but as a cosmological cycle. Most modern scholars believe the specific identification of Cortés with Quetzalcoatl was heavily amplified or invented in post-conquest sources — but the fact that 1519 was the calendrically significant Year One Reed would have been genuinely unsettling to anyone who could read the ritual calendar.

events.label: Eight Omens Before the Conquest
events.description: Aztec sources — recorded primarily in the Florentine Codex, compiled 50 years after the events — describe eight ominous signs in the decade before the Spanish arrival: a year-long comet, a self-igniting temple, a daylight comet, the lake boiling without fire, a weeping woman at night, and a bird with a mirror in its head showing warriors on unknown beasts.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Florentine Codex, compiled by Franciscan friar Bernardino de Sahagún from interviews with Aztec elders beginning in the 1540s, is the primary source for the eight omens. Scholars debate how much of the omen narrative was genuine pre-conquest tradition versus post-conquest reconstruction designed to explain why the Aztecs failed to resist more forcefully — a face-saving narrative of cosmic inevitability. The weeping woman who cries "my children, where shall I take you?" is one root of the later La Llorona legend, the weeping ghost woman in Mexican folklore.

events.label: Florentine Codex Compiled
events.description: Fray Bernardino de Sahagún systematically interviewed Aztec elders from the 1540s through the 1570s to produce the Florentine Codex — a 12-volume encyclopedia of Aztec culture in Nahuatl and Spanish covering religion, natural history, economics, and the conquest itself. It remains the single most important source on pre-conquest Aztec civilization.

events.label: Nezahualcoyotl's Legal Code
events.description: Around 1445, Nezahualcoyotl (neh-zah-wahl-KOH-yotl) — king of Texcoco and the empire's most brilliant administrator — formalized an 80-article legal code covering property, marriage, crime, and military conduct, creating the most sophisticated body of written law in pre-conquest Mesoamerica.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The code specified the death penalty for murder, adultery, theft by officials, and battlefield cowardice — and notably held nobles to harsher standards than commoners for the same offenses. Nezahualcoyotl reigned in Texcoco for 41 years (1431–1472), long enough to actually implement and refine his legal system rather than just promulgate it. His code was partially adopted across the Triple Alliance, making Texcoco the legal model for the empire even as Tenochtitlan dominated it militarily.

events.label: Albarradón of Nezahualcoyotl
events.description: The Albarradón de Nezahualcoyotl was a 10-mile stone dike built across Lake Texcoco after the 1449 flood, separating the brackish eastern waters from the freshwater western zone where Tenochtitlan's chinampa (floating garden) agriculture grew — the largest hydraulic engineering project in the pre-Columbian Americas.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The dike was sluice-gated, allowing controlled water exchange, not just a blunt wall. Without the freshwater separation it maintained, the chinampa fields that fed Tenochtitlan's hundreds of thousands of residents could not have survived salt intrusion. Nezahualcoyotl both designed and supervised the construction personally — an unusual combination of royal and engineering authority that reinforced his reputation as the most intellectually accomplished ruler of his generation.

events.label: Ixtlilxochitl I of Texcoco
events.description: Ruler of Texcoco and father of Nezahualcoyotl, Ixtlilxochitl I was murdered by the Tepanec tyrant Tezozomoc when Nezahualcoyotl was a teenager. His assassination left his son as a fugitive, hiding in the mountains while plotting his return — the formative trauma that shaped the philosopher-king of Texcoco.

events.label: Moquihuix of Tlatelolco
events.description: Last independent tlatoani of Tlatelolco, Moquihuix attempted to build an anti-Tenochtitlan coalition among rival city-states. Axayacatl crushed the revolt in 1473; Moquihuix died in the assault on Tlatelolco's Templo Mayor, ending the sister city's political independence and uniting the two island capitals under Tenochtitlan's rule.

events.label: Nanahuatzin and the Fifth Sun
events.description: The Aztec creation myth held that the current world — the Fifth Sun — was born at Teotihuacan when a humble, sore-covered god named Nanahuatzin leapt into a sacred fire without hesitation, becoming the sun, while the beautiful god Tecuciztecatl flinched and had to be shamed into the flames second, emerging only as the dimmer moon.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The sun still refused to move after its birth: it just sat fixed in the sky, demanding the sacrifice of all the other gods before it would begin its daily journey. The name Nanahuatzin literally means 'full of sores.' He is considered an aspect of Xolotl, the dog-headed deity associated with lightning and death — so the same god who guides the dead through the underworld also powers the sunrise.

events.label: Macuilxochitzin
events.description: Macuilxochitzin was a celebrated Nahuatl poet of the Aztec imperial period, daughter of the powerful cihuacoatl (chief advisor) Tlacaelel, and one of the very few pre-Columbian women whose literary work survives identified by name.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Her surviving poems include an eyewitness-style account of the Aztec war against the Tarascans (the Mexica's western rivals who defeated them badly around 1479), composed from the perspective of someone at the Tenochtitlan court receiving the news — an unusual female voice in a martial genre. The wikiExtract notes she was also the niece of the tlatoani Axayacatl, placing her at the absolute center of power. Her existence is cited by scholars as evidence of gender parallelism in Aztec elite culture: high-born women could achieve recognized intellectual standing, not just domestic roles.

events.label: Battle of Otumba
events.description: At the Battle of Otumba on July 7, 1520, Cortés's roughly 400 surviving Spaniards and a few thousand Tlaxcalan allies faced an Aztec army of around 40,000 on an open plain. Cortés's cavalry broke the Aztec center by killing the Aztec field commander and capturing his battle standard — in Mesoamerican military convention, the loss of the standard signaled defeat regardless of actual numbers, and the Aztec army withdrew.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The battle was decided not by sustained fighting but by a single cavalry charge aimed directly at the command cluster bearing the ornate standard (a towered feather-and-gold device carried on the commander's back). Cortés himself is credited in Spanish accounts with leading the charge. The Aztec force outnumbered the Spanish roughly 100 to 1, making this one of the most lopsided surviving battles of the conquest — and the one that saved the entire enterprise from total collapse.

events.label: Cantares Mexicanos
events.description: The Cantares Mexicanos is the largest surviving collection of Nahuatl poetry, compiled in the mid-16th century from pre-conquest oral tradition. Its 91 songs include warrior hymns, flower-songs, and the great laments for the fall of Tenochtitlan — including the lines the chapter quotes: "Broken spears lie in the roads / We have torn our hair in our grief."

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The manuscript contains over half of all known traditional Nahuatl songs and is currently held at the National Library of Mexico in Mexico City. Most pre-conquest pictorial books were destroyed during the conquest or in early colonial book-burnings — Spanish friars considered them the devil's work — making the Cantares, compiled by indigenous informants working with colonial-era scholars, one of the only windows into the Aztec literary tradition. The poetry it preserves includes verses attributed to Nezahualcoyotl, the poet-king of Texcoco.
